headings.title: Introduction to Inferential Statistics in Nursing Research
headings.content: Inferential statistics allow researchers to take data collected from a small group and make generalizations about a much larger group. While descriptive statistics simply summarize numbers, inferential tools test theories and evaluate whether observed differences happen by chance or reflect real clinical effects. In Nigerian nursing research, running a full census of every patient in a state is practically impossible due to resource and time limits. Drawing conclusions from a smaller subset solves this challenge.

headings.title: Populations and Samples: The Basis of Inference
headings.content: A population includes every single member of the group you want to study, such as all diabetic patients admitted to federal teaching hospitals in Nigeria. A sample is a smaller, manageable subset chosen from that population. For inference to work properly, the sample must accurately reflect the larger group. Random selection helps minimize bias, ensuring that the results obtained from the ward or clinic can safely apply to patients nationwide.

headings.title: Formulating Research and Statistical Hypotheses
headings.content:
Hypothesis testing starts by setting up two opposing statements that guide data analysis. 

- **Null Hypothesis ($H_0$)**: States that there is no real difference, relationship, or effect in the population.
- **Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$ or $H_a$)**: States that a real difference, relationship, or effect does exist in the population.

Statistical tests are designed to evaluate the null hypothesis, checking whether data provides enough evidence to reject it.

headings.title: Understanding P-Values and Significance Levels
headings.content: The **p-value** (probability value) tells you the likelihood that your results occurred purely by chance. Researchers set a threshold beforehand called the significance level, commonly written as alpha ($\alpha$), usually set at 0.05. If your calculated p-value falls below 0.05, you reject the null hypothesis because the finding is considered statistically significant. A common misconception treats the p-value as the probability that your hypothesis is wrong, when it actually measures how compatible your data is with the null hypothesis.

headings.title: Type I and Type II Errors in Clinical Decision Making
headings.content:
Statistical testing is not infallible, and conclusions can sometimes lead us astray.

| Error Type | Description | Clinical Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Type I Error ($\alpha$)** | Rejecting a true null hypothesis (False Positive) | Adopting an ineffective or harmful nursing intervention |
| **Type II Error ($\beta$)** | Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (False Negative) | Rejecting a beneficial nursing intervention that actually works |

Balancing these errors requires careful sample size calculation before launching a clinical trial.

headings.title: Common Parametric Tests: t-Tests and ANOVA
headings.content:
Parametric tests are used when data is normally distributed and measured on interval or ratio scales. 

- **Independent samples t-test**: Compares the mean scores of two separate groups, such as average blood pressure between male and female hypertensive patients.
- **Paired t-test**: Compares mean scores from the same group at two different times, like pre-test and post-test pain scores after an intervention.
- **Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)**: Compares the means of three or more groups simultaneously, such as recovery times across four different surgical wards.

Using these tests requires checking underlying assumptions like data normality.

headings.title: Non-Parametric Alternatives for Nursing Data
headings.content:
Not all clinical data fits a neat bell curve. When data is ordinal, nominal, or heavily skewed, parametric assumptions break down. Non-parametric tests do not assume a normal distribution and serve as robust alternatives.

- **Mann-Whitney U test**: Compares two independent groups using ranked data instead of raw means.
- **Wilcoxon signed-rank test**: Compares two related measurements from the same group for ordinal or non-normal data.
- **Chi-Square test**: Analyzes categorical frequency data, such as comparing the proportion of smokers versus non-smokers who develop lung complications.

headings.title: Interpreting Results for Evidence-Based Nursing Practice
headings.content: Translating statistical output into clinical action requires looking beyond statistical significance to evaluate clinical relevance. A p-value might prove that a new mouthwash lowers bacterial counts significantly, but if the actual reduction is negligible, it may not justify changing hospital policy. Nurses must appraise confidence intervals and effect sizes to determine if an intervention produces meaningful improvements for patients at the bedside.
